title: Out of the whirlwind (Job 38–39)
hook: God answers with stars, sea and wild goats: "Where wast thou?", and no explanation

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem went down into the mines and asked where wisdom could be found. Your line was where shall wisdom be found. Today, Job finally gets the hearing he asked for.

Chapter after chapter, Job has demanded it: let God come, let me lay out my case. And the friends have answered for God, again and again. Then, after all of it: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said." A voice out of the storm. Job has his speech ready. The reader has questions too: will God mention the adversary, the test, the children, the boils? Will God explain? And the first thing God does is ask a question back.
screen: `JOB DEMANDED A HEARING.` → `A VOICE OUT OF THE STORM.` → `WILL GOD EXPLAIN?`

segments.voice: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Then the questions keep coming. Who measured the earth, stretched the line on it, laid its cornerstone, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut in the sea with doors, and told it, "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Have you walked the springs of the sea, or seen the storehouses of the snow? Can you bind the Pleiades, or loosen the bands of Orion? Then the animals: the lioness hunting for her cubs, the raven's young crying for food. "Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth?" The wild donkey that laughs at the city, the ostrich, the horse, the hawk. And God sends rain "on the wilderness, wherein there is no man." Rain no human will ever see. Here's what God never says: nothing about the adversary or the test, no reason for the boils or the house that fell. Job asked why, and God answered with the universe. Some readers hear a rebuke: who are you to question me? Some hear a strange comfort: the world is far bigger than Job's pain, and God cares for corners no human has visited, wild goats giving birth on a cliff with no one watching. Both readings agree on one thing. Job asked for a hearing, and God came.
screen: `WHERE WAST THOU?` · `WHEN THE MORNING STARS SANG.` · `WILD GOATS, AND RAIN WHERE NO MAN IS.` · `NO EXPLANATION. GOD CAME.`

segments.voice: Find something you didn't make, the sky through a window, a tree, a bird, a weed in a crack, or if you can't move, picture the night sky. Let the whirlwind's questions come, where was I when this was made, who waters this, and let your own worries stand next to something much larger. If you pray, you can simply look, and let the looking be your prayer.
Pleiades, the star cluster God asks Job if he can bind, among the questions asked out of the whirlwind. Today's word.
Your line: where wast thou. No reasons were given, only the whole wide world. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read God's speeches from the whirlwind near the end of the book of Job, and Jewish readers have understood them in more than one way, as rebuke, as comfort, and as an answer that is God's presence rather than an explanation.

chat.says: When God finally answers Job, does God explain why all those bad things happened?
options: No. God asks about the stars, the sea and wild goats, and never mentions the test.
Yes. God tells Job all about the adversary's bet and why it was allowed.
No. God stays silent the whole time, and Job is left with no answer at all.
chat.meaning: Out of the whirlwind God asks, Where wast thou? and speaks of stars, sea and animals, but says nothing about the adversary or the test.

Pleiades.meaning: a star cluster; kimah in the Hebrew of Job

Orion.meaning: a constellation; kesil in the Hebrew of Job

adversary.meaning: ha-satan, the accuser from the book's first chapter
